Repairs Meant to Be Seen

Visible mending—a method of repairing clothing with deliberately noticeable stitches and patches—turn[1] worn fabric into a surface for new design. A contrasting thread may trace the edge of a tear, while a patterned patch can reinforce a thinning elbow. The repair remains functional, but it also records where and how a garment has been used.

Although visible mending draws on traditional sewing techniques, it is not merely damage covered by bright cloth, but instead it is[2] a design shaped around the damaged area. Makers may induct[3] geometric rows of stitches, irregular patches cut from saved fabric, or colors chosen to echo another part of the garment. Some menders plan every stitch on paper, while others adjust the pattern as they encounter weak threads.[4]

Once commonly treated as a private household task, decorative repair is increasingly practiced in public.[5] Libraries host repair circles, clothing shops offer workshops, and online groups exchange photographs of techniques. These gatherings make repair knowledge easier to share—and make a repaired sleeve a visible choice rather than something to conceal.
